settings.question: Is this sashimi grade?
settings.answer:
There is no official or regulated definition of “sashimi-grade” or “sushi-grade” fish in the United States. Sellers use the terms to signal that fish is safe to eat raw, but they are not a certification or a legal standard. So here is ours.

All of our seafood is vacuum sealed and blast frozen to -10 °F at peak freshness, which preserves taste, texture and colour, and is processed in an accredited facility. It is lab tested for mercury and microplastics. Farmed fish raised on formulated feed are exempt from the FDA Food Code’s parasite-freezing rule, and we blast-freeze at harvest anyway. That is what sashimi-grade means to us.

There is always some risk in eating anything raw or undercooked. If you are concerned or particularly sensitive, consult your doctor. The FDA conservatively suggests cooking to an internal temperature of 145 °F.

settings.question: Is your seafood mercury free?
settings.answer:
Most fish naturally contain trace amounts of mercury, and it is close to impossible to find seafood that is genuinely “mercury free.” Mercury can sit below what a test can detect, so “mercury free” may not be true even when a result reads zero.

That is why we talk about mercury safe instead, and why we define it: our standard is 0.1 ppm methylmercury or below, a tenth of the FDA’s 1.0 ppm action level. Every supplier is tested against that standard before we approve them, then audited at random to make sure they stay compliant.

We also test selenium and look at the selenium-to-mercury ratio, because selenium in fish binds mercury so that less of it is absorbed.

FDA and EPA recommend 2 to 3 servings a week, 4 oz each, from their “Best Choices” list for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Salmon is on that list.

settings.question: What counts as a serving?
settings.answer:
We consider one portion to be 4 to 6 ounces of cooked fish, which matches the FDA’s definition of a serving of seafood. That is the guideline behind how much fish by weight goes into a box described in servings. Some of our fish, such as king salmon, come in larger pieces of 7.5 to 8.5 oz, so a single piece can be two nutritional servings.

Many of our members work with a nutritionist or practitioner, or use an app, to decide what they should be eating for protein, fats or specific nutrients. The right amount and frequency for you is personal, and our job is to give you the data that makes the decision easy.
